newsitem.title: CHINA: Death clouds future for privileged Deng offspring.
newsitem.headline: Death clouds future for privileged Deng offspring.

text.p: They flit about the globe with a freedom few Chinese dare dream of, popping up in Tokyo for an art show, New York for a book signing, Sydney for a fundraiser, or tending their business empires in Hong Kong.
They are Deng Xiaoping's children and have prospered despite business failures and regular brushes with corruption scandals.
Empowered by the immense clout of China's paramount leader, they have been among the country's most prominent "princelings" -- privileged offspring of the Communist Party leadership.
That all may have changed at 9.08 p.m. on Wednesday when the key to their high-flying fortunes died after years of decline.
"People did business with them because of the Deng connection," said Hong Kong Deng-watcher Tai Ming Cheung.
"I think they will continue to have some privileges, but this will decline. After Mao died, his children faded quickly and were out of the picture within a year."

Though Deng held no official titles in recent years, he was the closest thing modern China had to an emperor, ensuring that his wife and children were accorded enormous deference and freedom wherever they went.

In the 1990s, as the faltering Deng slipped into seclusion, reporters in Hong Kong and Taiwan hounded Deng's children as if they were rock stars -- eager for the slightest hint about the old man's health and, in turn, China's future.
The children have used the family fame to great advantage, although as Deng's mental faculties faded after 1994, rivals have begun to shed their reticence to take on the first family.
Arguably closest to Deng was daughter Deng Rong, who in 1995 promoted her best-selling biography "My Father, Deng Xiaoping" with high-profile book tours of America, Europe and Asia.

Deng Rong was always at her father's side as handler, nurse and interpreter. Her practice of shouting interlocutors' words into his one good ear and interpreting his gravelly, softspoken Sichuanese into Mandarin or English led many experts to assume that she was able to control Deng's view of the world.

Yet rumours have long swirled in Beijing that Deng Rong was too independent and too close to her U.S. and Japanese backers to be trusted. On the eve of Deng's death, Beijing disbanded his personal office, which she had used as a power base.

Things could get worse. Deng Rong's business empire was shaken in 1996 when U.S. inquiries into Chinese arms smuggling led to Poly Technologies in Beijing, a People's Liberation Army company that is headed by her husband, He Ping.
"The connections that he has will serve He Ping well because the Chinese people still see Deng as a surrogate mother," said Andrew Yang, a military analyst in Taipei.
"But that could change if he oversteps the proper bounds."
The Deng limelight has not ensured success in the capitalist world, entry to which was made possible by Deng's reforms.

Son Deng Zhifang quietly quit as vice-chairman of a listed Hong Kong subsidiary of giant Capital Iron & Steel after the subsidiary's chairman Zhou Beifang -- another princeling whose father was a crony of Deng Xiaoping -- was arrested for graft.
Eldest son Deng Pufang is still haunted by Beijing's closure of his investment firm Kang Hua in the 1980s for profiteering in an early anti-corruption drive ordered by his father.

Analysts said China was unlikely to use Deng's death to press charges against Deng Zhifang or Deng Pufang, a paraplegic who was hurt in a mysterious fall from a window when his father was under attack during the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution.
"In the short term, I don't see any campaign to go after them," Tai said. "But if they try to push their position to make use of the Deng name, it may go against them."
Since the Kang Hua debacle, Deng Pufang has devoted himself to a national disabled charity.
Daughter Deng Lin probably has fared best, milking the Deng name to nurture her own career as a painter while her husband, Wu Jianchang, did the same to build a Hong Kong business empire.
Wu controls several listed firms linked to state-run giant China Nonferrous Metals Import and Export Corp but was sacked from the board of one in 1996 at shareholders' insistence.

Only one Deng offspring has followed her father into politics. Deng Nan is vice-minister of the cabinet's State Science and Technology Commission and is married to another career technocrat, Zhang Hong.
